title: Judges 16:23–31
context: The Philistine lords gather in the temple of Dagon to celebrate their god's supposed victory over Samson, and they call the blinded prisoner out to entertain them. Samson asks to lean on the pillars, prays to the LORD to remember him and strengthen him once more, and pulls the house down on the lords and the crowd, dying with them. His family buries him in his father's tomb. Judges records his death soberly; the outcome is God's victory over Dagon, even through a flawed and broken judge.

verses.text: The lords of the Philistines gathered together to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god, and to rejoice; for they said, “Our god has delivered Samson our enemy into our hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: The lords offer "a great sacrifice to Dagon their god," crediting him with Samson's capture. Arminian readers see the stakes become openly theological: the question is now whether the LORD or Dagon is God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Samson's fall has brought dishonor on the LORD's name before the nations. The scene is set for God to vindicate his own glory, as he later does again when Dagon falls before the ark (1 Samuel 5:3–4).

verses.text: When the people saw him, they praised their god; for they said, “Our god has delivered our enemy and the destroyer of our country, who has slain many of us, into our hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: The people praise their god for delivering "the destroyer of our country." Arminian readers note the shame of a servant whose sin gave occasion for pagan worship, a reminder that our conduct reflects on God's name.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Philistines' praise is misplaced; the LORD, not Dagon, gave Samson into their hand because of Samson's sin. God remains sovereign even over the enemy's apparent victory.

verses.text: When their hearts were merry, they said, “Call for Samson, that he may entertain us.” They called for Samson out of the prison; and he performed before them. They set him between the pillars;
verses.arminianNotes: With merry hearts they call Samson out to entertain them and set him between the pillars. Arminian readers see the depth of his humiliation, the once-mighty judge now a public spectacle for his enemies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that the Philistines themselves place Samson where God will use him. Human mockery unwittingly sets the stage for divine judgment, a recurring pattern in Scripture.

verses.text: and Samson said to the boy who held him by the hand, “Allow me to feel the pillars on which the house rests, that I may lean on them.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samson asks the boy leading him to let him feel the pillars. Arminian readers note that the blinded judge now depends on a child's hand, and that his request shows a deliberate, settled resolve.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the quiet preparation before the final act. God's purposes often advance through small, unnoticed details, here a request to a servant boy that no one around him understands.

verses.text: Now the house was full of men and women; and all the lords of the Philistines were there; and there were on the roof about three thousand men and women, who saw while Samson performed.
verses.arminianNotes: The house is full, with all the lords present and about three thousand on the roof watching. Arminian readers note the scale of the gathering, showing how fully the Philistine leadership has staked its honor on Dagon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the whole leadership of the oppressors is gathered in one place. God brings the enemies of his people together for a judgment that will break their power and expose their god.

verses.text: Samson called to the LORD, and said, “Lord GOD, remember me, please, and strengthen me, please, only this once, God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes.”
verses.arminianNotes: "Lord GOD, remember me, please, and strengthen me, please, only this once." Arminian readers see a humbled man turning to God in prayer, his plea answered; they also note his request still centers on vengeance "for my two eyes."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note both the humility of the prayer and the personal motive. Both traditions see God answering a flawed servant's cry, using Samson's request to accomplish judgment on Dagon's worshipers.

verses.text: Samson took hold of the two middle pillars on which the house rested and leaned on them, the one with his right hand and the other with his left.
verses.arminianNotes: Samson grips the two middle pillars, one with each hand. Arminian readers see a final act of faith in which his choice and God's empowering work together, an act Hebrews 11:34 may echo: "from weakness were made strong."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see God's strength made perfect in weakness. A blind captive becomes the instrument of God's victory, so that the glory belongs plainly to God rather than to Samson's own might.

verses.text: Samson said, “Let me die with the Philistines!” He bowed himself with all his might; and the house fell on the lords, and on all the people who were in it. So the dead that he killed at his death were more than those who he killed in his life.
verses.arminianNotes: "Let me die with the Philistines!" The house falls, and he kills more at his death than in his life. Arminian readers read this not as an endorsement of taking one's life but as a warrior's death in battle against God's enemies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also read Samson's death as an act of judgment and sacrifice in battle, not as a model for self-harm. Both traditions see God's power at work and the irony of a deliverer who wins most fully in his death.

verses.text: Then his brothers and all the house of his father came down and took him, and brought him up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the burial site of Manoah his father. He judged Israel twenty years.
verses.arminianNotes: His family buries him "between Zorah and Eshtaol," where the Spirit first moved him (13:25). Arminian readers see a life of great gifts and real failures brought home, a sober lesson in faithfulness and its absence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repeated summary, "He judged Israel twenty years" (compare 15:20). Samson's story ends where it began, a reminder that God's grace raised him up and carried his flawed life to its purpose.
